Intransigence

in-TRAN-si-jents · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Intransigence is the refusal to compromise.

Years of intransigence on both sides doomed the peace talks -- neither delegation would give an inch on a single demand.

Worked Example

The homeowners' association's intransigence over the fence height turned a simple disagreement into a three-year legal battle.

Intransigence names the stubborn, unyielding stance itself, usually in a negotiation or dispute where some flexibility is expected.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stubbornness: unwillingness to change one's position

inflexibility: an unwillingness to bend or adapt

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flexibility: willingness to adapt or compromise

cooperation: working together willingly

Where it sits · how much harm the refusal causes — stubbornness → intransigence → intransigence

stubbornness vs. intransigence: A little stubbornness over which restaurant to pick is harmless.

intransigence vs. intransigence: Real intransigence in a hostage negotiation can cost lives.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root+suffix — transigence

root+suffix — transigence: willingness to settle or compromise (Latin (transigere))

Put it together

Put it together: in- ("not") + transigence ("willingness to settle") = a refusal to compromise or come to terms.

Use the root in a new word: transaction

Use the root in a new word: transaction: The same root, transigere ("to drive a deal through"), survives in the everyday word "transaction" -- a deal or exchange.

Root Check

Word Choice

Intransigence describes a refusal to compromise in a negotiation or dispute -- a procedural, often political stance. Implacable describes a more personal, emotional refusal to forgive.
